--- title: "Multinomial Model" description: "Modeling the counts of outcomes across multiple categorical trials." categories: [Regression, GLM, Classification] image: "Figures/9.png" order: 11 reading-time: true --- ## General Principles To model the relationship between a vector outcome variable in which each element of the vector is a frequency from a set of more than two categories and one or more independent variables, we can use a _Multinomial_ model. ## Considerations ::: callout-note - We have the same considerations as for the [Categorical model](10. Categorical model.qmd). ::: ## Example Below is an example code snippet demonstrating a Bayesian multinomial model using the BayesForge (BF) package. This example is based on @mcelreath2018statistical. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {#1bca0e82 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from BayesForge import bf import jax.numpy as jnp import jax # Setup device ------------------------------------------------ m = bf('cpu') # Import Data & Data Manipulation ------------------------------------------------ # Import data_path = m.load.sim_multinomial(only_path=True) m.data(data_path, sep=',') # Define model ------------------------------------------------ def model(income, career): # Parameter prior distributions alpha = m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(2,), name='a') beta = m.dist.half_normal(0.5, shape=(1,), name='b') s_1 = alpha[0] + beta * income[0] s_2 = alpha[1] + beta * income[1] s_3 = [0] p = jnp.exp(jnp.stack([s_1[0], s_2[0], s_3[0]])) # Likelihood m.dist.multinomial(probs = p[career], obs=career) # Run sampler ------------------------------------------------ m.fit(model, progress_bar=False) # Summary ------------------------------------------------ m.summary() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` /home/sosa/work/3.12venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/tqdm/auto.py:21: TqdmWarning: IProgress not found. Julia ```julia using PyBayesForge # Setup device------------------------------------------------ m = importBF(platform="cpu") # Import Data & Data Manipulation ------------------------------------------------ # Import data_path = m.load.sim_multinomial(only_path = true) m.data(data_path, sep=',') # Define model ------------------------------------------------ @BF function model(income, career) # Parameter prior distributions alpha = m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(2,), name='a') beta = m.dist.half_normal(0.5, shape=(1,), name='b') s_1 = alpha[0] + beta * income[0] s_2 = alpha[1] + beta * income[1] # ⚠️ Use jnp.array to create a Python object, so [0] indexing works s_3 = jnp.array([0.0]) p = jnp.exp(jnp.stack([s_1[0], s_2[0], s_3[0]])) # Likelihood m.dist.multinomial(probs = p[career], obs=career) end # Run mcmc ------------------------------------------------ m.fit(model) # Optimize model parameters through MCMC sampling # Summary ------------------------------------------------ m.summary() # Get posterior distributions ``` ::: ## Mathematical Details We can model a vector of frequencies using a Dirichlet distribution. For an outcome variable $Y_i$ with $K$ categories, the *Dirichlet* likelihood function is: $$ Y_i \sim \text{Multinomial}(\theta_i) \\ \theta_i = \text{Softmax}(\phi_i) \\ \phi_{[i,1]} = \alpha_1 + \beta_1 X_i \\ \phi_{[i,2]} = \alpha_2 + \beta_2 X_i \\ ... \\ \phi_{[i,k]} = 0 \\ \alpha_{k} \sim \text{Normal}(0,1) \\ \beta_{k} \sim \text{Normal}(0.1) $$ Where: - $Y_i$ is the outcome (i.e. the vector of frequencies for each $k$ categories) for observation *i*. - $\theta_i$ is a vector unique to each observation, *i*, which gives the probability of observing *i* in category *k*. - $\phi_i$ give the linear model for each of the $k$ categories. Note that we use the softmax function to ensure that that the probabilities $\theta_i$ form a [simplex 🛈]{#simplex}. - Each element of $\phi_i$ is obtained by applying a linear regression model with its own respective intercept $\alpha_k$ and slope coefficient $\beta_k$. To ensure the model is identifiable, one category, *K*, is arbitrarily chosen as a reference or baseline category. The linear predictor for this reference category is set to zero. The coefficients for the other categories then represent the change in the log-odds of being in that category versus the reference category. ## Model validation tests - [Comparison with Stan](https://github.com/BGN-for-ASNA/BF/tree/main/Test/4.%20Rethinking/Numpyro%20backend): `8.Multinomial.py` fits the same model with BayesForge and Stan and compares the posterior distributions (KL divergence). - [Documentation example](https://github.com/BGN-for-ASNA/BF/tree/main/Test/3.Documentation/Python): the Python example of this page is run by the documentation tests (`test_model_pages.py`). ## Reference(s)
